title: Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
abstract-summary: Under equal thinking-token budgets single-agent LLMs match or outperform multi-agent systems across Qwen3 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama and Gemini 2.5; information-theoretic argument via Data Processing Inequality shows single agents are more information-efficient
notes: Core frontier-model-paradox evidence: when compute is controlled multi-agent gains vanish; predicted by Data Processing Inequality

title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
authors: Jieyu Kim, Yicheng Wang, Zhi Huang, Qian Liu
abstract-summary: Proposes taxonomy for scaling agent systems; finds coordination yields diminishing returns once single-agent success rate exceeds ~45%; multi-agent relative gain ranges from +80.8% to -70.0% depending on task decomposability
notes: Key finding: once SA baseline >45% adding agents yields diminishing or negative returns; directly supports frontier-model paradox

title: Beyond the Strongest LLM: Multi-Turn Multi-Agent Orchestration vs. Single LLMs on Benchmarks
authors: Ruihan Xiao, Yue Zhang, et al.
abstract-summary: Multi-turn multi-agent orchestration matches or slightly exceeds strongest single model on GPQA-Diamond IFEval MuSR; ablations reveal herding effects and premature consensus
reported-value-ma: orchestration matches or slightly exceeds best single LLM
backbone-model: Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4, Claude Sonnet 4
notes: Partial counter-evidence: orchestration still slightly helps but gap is narrow with frontier models; herding can hurt

title: Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?
authors: Jiayi Chen, Yuxiang Zhang, et al.
abstract-summary: Benefits of MAS over SAS diminish as LLM capabilities improve; proposes hybrid request-cascading paradigm improving accuracy 1.1-12% while reducing costs up to 20%
notes: Directly states frontier-model paradox: MAS is workaround for LLM limits that becomes less needed as models improve; proposes hybrid solution

title: AgentArch: A Comprehensive Benchmark to Evaluate Agent Architectures in Enterprise
authors: Tara Bogavelli, Roshnee Sharma, Hari Subramani
abstract-summary: First benchmark systematically evaluating 18 agentic architectures across 6 LLMs on enterprise tasks; reveals model-specific architectural preferences challenging one-size-fits-all paradigm
notes: Shows significant weaknesses in multi-agent ReAct; architectural preference is model-dependent supporting nuanced view of frontier-model paradox

title: Understanding Agent Scaling in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems via Diversity
abstract-summary: Homogeneous agent scaling shows strong diminishing returns; marginal gain per additional agent collapses toward zero; diversity is key to maintaining scaling benefits
notes: Information-theoretic explanation for diminishing returns in homogeneous MAS; supports frontier-model paradox for same-model scaling

title: Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration
authors: Chen Qian, Zihao Xie, et al.
abstract-summary: Multi-agent performance follows logistic growth with agent count; collaborative emergence occurs earlier than neural emergence; majority voting gains plateau at ~8 agents with only 0.9% improvement
notes: Early evidence of diminishing returns: voting plateaus quickly; logistic growth pattern suggests ceiling with stronger models

title: Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
authors: Andries P Smit, Nathan Grinsztajn, Paul Duckworth, Thomas D Barrett, A Pretorius
abstract-summary: MAD does not reliably outperform self-consistency and ensembling; debate systems are more sensitive to hyperparameters; benefits are not inherent to multi-agent architecture
reported-value-ma: MAD does not reliably outperform alternatives
notes: Supports frontier-model paradox: simpler single-agent methods like self-consistency match or beat MAD; architectural overhead not justified

title: Debate Only When Necessary: Adaptive Multiagent Collaboration for Efficient LLM Reasoning
authors: Sugyeong Eo, Hyeonseok Moon, Evelyn Hayoon Zi, Chanjun Park, Heuiseok Lim
abstract-summary: Proposes DOWN framework: selective debate activation based on confidence scores; 6x efficiency improvement while preserving performance; unnecessary debate increases error risk
reported-value-ma: matches full debate with 6x fewer interactions
notes: Shows most queries don't need multi-agent debate; stronger models have higher initial confidence reducing debate need further -- supports paradox

title: System Card: Claude Opus 4.6
abstract-summary: Opus 4.6 achieves 65.4% Terminal-Bench 2.0 (max effort) 80.8% SWE-bench Verified; leads GDPval-AA by 190 Elo over Opus 4.5 and 144 over GPT-5.2; SOTA on WebArena OSWorld BrowseComp
notes: Single-agent frontier model achieving SOTA across multiple agentic benchmarks; demonstrates capabilities that previously required multi-agent systems

title: Introducing Claude 4 (System Card: Claude Opus 4 & Sonnet 4)
abstract-summary: Opus 4 achieves 72.5% SWE-bench 43.2% Terminal-bench; best coding model at launch; designed for sustained multi-step reasoning and long-horizon planning
notes: Baseline for tracking single-agent frontier progress; Opus 4 to 4.6 shows 72.5% to 80.8% on SWE-bench purely from model improvements

title: System Card: Claude Opus 4.5
abstract-summary: Opus 4.5 achieves SOTA on WebArena (single-agent) 62.3% MCP-Atlas; 15% improvement over Sonnet 4.5 on Terminal-Bench; 80.9% SWE-bench Verified
notes: Explicitly notes single-agent SOTA on WebArena; multi-agent systems with specialized prompts score higher but are not directly comparable

title: Raising the bar on SWE-bench Verified with Claude 3.5 Sonnet
abstract-summary: Upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves 49% on SWE-bench Verified beating previous SOTA of 45%; design philosophy emphasized minimal scaffolding giving control to the model itself
notes: Design philosophy of minimal scaffolding directly supports frontier-model paradox: stronger model needs less orchestration infrastructure

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
authors: Carlos E Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik R Narasimhan
abstract-summary: Introduces SWE-bench with 2294 software engineering problems from real GitHub issues; establishes evaluation framework for coding agents; initial models solved only 1.96% of problems
notes: Foundational benchmark; trajectory from 1.96% to 93.9% illustrates how model improvement reduces need for complex multi-agent scaffolding

title: SWE-ABS: Adversarial Benchmark Strengthening Exposes Inflated Success Rates on Test-based Benchmark
authors: Boxi Yu, Yang Cao, et al.
abstract-summary: 19.78% of top-30 SWE-bench solutions are semantically incorrect; strengthened tests reduce top agent from 78.8% to 62.2%; exposes evaluation inflation
notes: Important methodological caution: inflated SWE-bench scores may overstate frontier single-agent progress; tempers paradox claims

title: SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement
authors: Antonis Antoniades, Albert Orwall, Kexun Zhang, Yuxi Xie, Anirudh Goyal, William Wang
abstract-summary: Integrates MCTS with LLM agents for software engineering tasks; hybrid value function with self-improvement mechanism; enables backtracking and exploration of alternatives
notes: Shows sophisticated single-agent search (MCTS) can substitute for multi-agent coordination; supports paradox by replacing multi-agent with smarter search

title: From 80% to 93.9%: Why the Claude Mythos SWE-Bench Jump Matters
abstract-summary: Claude Mythos achieves 93.9% on SWE-bench Verified up from 80% Opus 4.6; represents massive single-model improvement on complex software engineering tasks
notes: Strongest single-agent result to date; 93.9% eliminates most need for multi-agent approaches on this benchmark

title: FeatureBench: Benchmarking Agentic Coding for Complex Feature Development
abstract-summary: 200 tasks from 24 repos; Claude 4.5 Opus achieves only 11.0% despite 74.4% on SWE-bench; exposes gap between bug-fixing and feature development for agentic models
notes: Counter-evidence: even frontier models struggle on complex feature dev; suggests multi-agent approaches may still help for harder task types

title: APEX-SWE
abstract-summary: Benchmarks cross-system integration and observability (84% of real dev work); Claude Opus 4.6 tops at 40.5% Pass@1; all models fail reliably on real-world integration tasks
notes: Shows frontier models still limited on integration tasks beyond single-repo bug fixes; multi-agent might still help for cross-system work

title: The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs
authors: Akshit Sinha, Arvindh Arun, Shashwat Goel, Steffen Staab, Jonas Geiping
abstract-summary: Marginal gains in single-step accuracy compound into exponential improvements for long-horizon tasks; larger models execute significantly more turns correctly; self-conditioning error effect identified
notes: Supports paradox: seemingly small model improvements have outsized effects on complex tasks reducing multi-agent need; self-conditioning errors compound in MAS too

title: MAESTRO: Multi-Agent Evaluation Suite for Testing Reliability and Observability
abstract-summary: 12 representative MAS across popular frameworks; MAS architecture dominates resource profiles more than backend model choice; substantial run-to-run variance in performance
notes: MAS architecture matters more than model choice; high variance undermines reliability; supports argument that simpler single-agent may be more predictable

title: MASEval: Extending Multi-Agent Evaluation from Models to Systems
abstract-summary: Framework choice matters as much as model choice across 3 benchmarks 3 models 3 frameworks; universal evaluation interface for any agent on any benchmark
notes: Highlights that MAS performance is confounded by framework effects; harder to attribute gains to multi-agent architecture vs engineering

title: Silo-Bench: A Scalable Environment for Evaluating Distributed Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract-summary: 30 tasks across 3 communication complexity levels; 54 configurations 1620 experiments; agents form correct coordination topologies but fail at reasoning integration; coordination overhead eliminates parallelization gains at scale
notes: Communication-Reasoning Gap: agents coordinate well but can't integrate distributed state; coordination overhead scales worse than model improvement

title: SWE-Compass: Towards Unified Evaluation of Agentic Coding Abilities for Large Language Models
abstract-summary: 2000 instances across 8 task types 10 languages; Claude-Sonnet-4 ranks first under both SWE-Agent (31.8%) and Claude Code (32.9%); reveals hierarchy of difficulty across tasks
notes: Shows single-agent performance varies significantly by task type; some areas still low enough that MAS could help

title: Auto-scaling LLM-based multi-agent systems through dynamic integration of agents
authors: Ravindu Perera, Anuradha Basnayake, Manjusri Wickramasinghe
abstract-summary: Dynamic Real-Time Agent Generation (DRTAG) outperforms static MAS; automatic creation and integration of new agents driven by task context
notes: Shows dynamic MAS can outperform static MAS but does not compare against single frontier agent; architectural improvement within MAS paradigm

title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
abstract-summary: Modular benchmark for multi-agent collaboration and competition; graph topology performs best; cognitive planning improves milestone rates by 3%; GPT-4o-mini achieves highest average task score
notes: Smaller model (GPT-4o-mini) outperforms larger ones in multi-agent setting; suggests model size alone doesn't determine MAS effectiveness
